goals: Explain the meaning of unicameral and bicameral legislatures
Name the States that have a Legislative Council, as of 2024, and say how a Council is created or abolished
Describe the composition and term of the Legislative Assembly and how its members are elected
State the qualifications for membership and name the presiding officers of the Assembly

slides.heading: The State Legislature: Assembly and Council
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **how many Houses**, and the **Legislative Assembly**.

nodes.label: One House or two
Assembly: composition and term
Qualifications
Speaker and Deputy Speaker

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: unicameral and bicameral legislatures, the composition and term of the Legislative Assembly, its qualifications for membership, and its presiding officers
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every State in India has a legislature that makes laws for the State. Some have one House and some have two. In this part we see which is which, and then study the Legislative Assembly, the directly elected House: its size, its term, who may become a member, and who presides over it.

slides.heading: Where the State legislature fits
slides.body_md: The legislature is the **lawmaking body** of the State.

nodes.label: Voters elect the Assembly
Assembly makes laws and controls the ministry
Governor gives assent to bills

visual.alt: Flow: voters elect the Legislative Assembly, the Assembly makes laws and controls the ministry, and the Governor gives assent to bills
visual.caption: Where the State legislature fits.

slides.narration: In each State, the voters elect the Legislative Assembly. The Assembly makes laws and keeps watch over the ministry. When a bill has passed, the Governor gives assent and it becomes a law. In this chapter we are studying this lawmaking body, which in some States has one House and in others has two.

slides.heading: Unicameral and bicameral
bullets: **Unicameral:** one House, the Legislative Assembly.
**Bicameral:** two Houses, the Assembly and the Legislative Council.
The Assembly is the **lower House**; the Council is the **upper House**.

visual.alt: Two panels. A unicameral State legislature has one House, the directly elected Legislative Assembly. A bicameral State legislature has two Houses: the Legislative Council as the upper House, mostly indirectly elected, and the Legislative Assembly as the lower House, directly elected
visual.caption: One House or two (schematic).

slides.narration: A unicameral legislature has only one House, the Legislative Assembly, or Vidhan Sabha. A bicameral legislature has two Houses. The second is the Legislative Council, or Vidhan Parishad. The Assembly is called the lower House because it is directly elected and more powerful, and the Council is called the upper House.

slides.heading: Which States have a Council?
slides.body_md: Only **six** States, as of 2024.

visual.alt: Table: as of 2024 six States have a Legislative Council and are bicameral: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh; all the other States are unicameral
visual.caption: Six bicameral States, as of 2024.

slides.narration: As of two thousand twenty four, six States have a Legislative Council. They are Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. All the other States have only an Assembly. Remember to write as of two thousand twenty four, because a Council can be created or abolished, and the list can change.

slides.heading: Quick check: one House
slides.body_md: Choose the correct term.
slides.narration: Read the question and think about how many Houses are described. Then choose the term for that number.

slides.heading: Creating or abolishing a Council
slides.body_md: A State cannot add or remove a Council on its own.

nodes.label: Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority
Parliament makes a law
Council is created or abolished

visual.alt: Flow: the State Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority, Parliament makes a law, and the Council is created or abolished
visual.caption: Creating or abolishing a Council.

slides.narration: The decision begins in the State. The Legislative Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority, asking for a Council to be created or abolished. But the State cannot finish the job alone. Parliament must then make a law. The same two steps work in both directions, for creating a Council and for abolishing it.

slides.heading: Is a second House worth having?
slides.body_md: People argue on both sides.

rows: A second look at hasty bills
Not chosen directly by all voters

visual.alt: Table of arguments about a Legislative Council: in favour are a second look at bills, room for experienced persons and wider representation; against are extra cost, delay and no direct election by all voters
visual.caption: Arguments sometimes made.

slides.narration: Supporters say a Council gives a second look at bills passed in a hurry, and makes room for experienced people who may never contest an election. Critics say a Council costs more to run, can slow down useful laws, and is not chosen directly by all the voters. In exams, give at least one point on each side.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting imagined States
slides.body_md: Count the Houses, then name the type.
bullets: Step 1 — Find out how many Houses the State has now.
Step 2 — One House means unicameral; two means bicameral.
Step 3 — A plan for a Council does not change the answer today.
Step 4 — Write the type with a reason.

visual.alt: Table sorting three imagined States: Tamrapur has an Assembly only and is unicameral, Girivan has an Assembly and a Council and is bicameral, and Sindhuvan has an Assembly only for now and is unicameral for now
visual.caption: Sorting imagined States.

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. Count the Houses the State has today. One House means unicameral, and two means bicameral. A plan to create a Council in the future does not change the answer today. So Tamrapur is unicameral, Girivan is bicameral, and Sindhuvan, which only plans a Council, is still unicameral for now.

slides.heading: The Legislative Assembly
bullets: Members are **directly elected** from territorial constituencies.
Strength: **not more than 500 and not less than 60**.
A few small States have fewer members by special provision.
Seats are **reserved** for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

rows: Not more than 500 and not less than 60 (a few small States have fewer)
For the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

visual.alt: Table of features of the Legislative Assembly: another name, strength of not more than 500 and not less than 60, direct election from territorial constituencies, reserved seats and a five-year term
visual.caption: The Assembly at a glance.

slides.narration: The Legislative Assembly, or Vidhan Sabha, is the House that the people elect directly. Each constituency elects one member. The number of members is not more than five hundred and not less than sixty, though a few small States have fewer by special provision. Some seats are reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.

slides.heading: The term of the Assembly
slides.body_md: The normal term is **five years**.

nodes.label: Elected for five years
Governor may dissolve earlier on the advice of the Chief Minister
Parliament may extend one year at a time in a national emergency

visual.alt: Flow: the Assembly is elected for five years, the Governor may dissolve it earlier on the advice of the Chief Minister, and Parliament may extend it one year at a time in a national emergency
visual.caption: The life of an Assembly.

slides.narration: The Assembly is elected for five years. But the term can change. The Governor can dissolve the Assembly earlier, acting in practice on the advice of the Chief Minister. And during a national emergency, Parliament can extend the term, one year at a time. After dissolution, fresh elections are held to form a new Assembly.

slides.heading: Quick check: the term
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank.
slides.narration: Remember the length of the normal term of an Assembly. Write the number of years.

slides.heading: Qualifications for membership
slides.body_md: Four basic conditions, in an **elementary** study.

rows: Must be a citizen of India
Must not hold a paid post under the government

visual.alt: Table of qualifications for membership of the Legislative Assembly: citizen of India, at least twenty-five years old, registered on the electoral roll, and no office of profit under the government
visual.caption: Four basic conditions.

slides.narration: To become a member of the Legislative Assembly a person must be a citizen of India, at least twenty five years old, and registered on the electoral roll. The person must also not hold an office of profit under the government. The law lists a few other disqualifications, but these four are the ones to learn.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is the candidate eligible?
slides.body_md: Test each candidate against the four conditions.
bullets: Step 1 — Check citizenship and the electoral roll.
Step 2 — Check the age: at least twenty-five.
Step 3 — Check whether the person holds a paid government post.
Step 4 — Give the answer with the failed condition.

rows: 31, citizen, on the roll, no paid post
45, citizen, on the roll, a paid government clerk

visual.alt: Table testing three imagined candidates: Arvind is eligible, Bhavna is not because she is below twenty-five, and Chitra is not because she holds an office of profit
visual.caption: Testing eligibility.

slides.narration: Test each person against the four conditions. Arvind is thirty one, a citizen and on the roll, with no paid post, so he is eligible. Bhavna is twenty two, below the minimum age. Chitra is forty five, but she is a government clerk, which is an office of profit. So the answer is no for both Bhavna and Chitra, and you must name the condition each fails.

slides.heading: Quick check: office of profit
slides.body_md: Apply the conditions to an imagined officer.
slides.narration: Think about the four conditions. Which one is broken by a person who works as a paid officer of the government?

slides.heading: Presiding officers
slides.body_md: The House elects its own presiding officers.

rows: Elected by the members from among themselves
Presides, keeps order, decides who speaks
Presides when the Speaker is absent

visual.alt: Table of presiding officers of the Assembly: the Speaker is elected by the members and presides and keeps order; the Deputy Speaker is elected by the members and presides when the Speaker is absent
visual.caption: Presiding officers.

slides.narration: The members of the Assembly elect a Speaker from among themselves. The Speaker presides over the House, keeps order and decides who may speak. The members also elect a Deputy Speaker, who presides when the Speaker is absent. The Speaker is not nominated by the Governor, and this is a common mistake in answers.

slides.heading: Quick check: restoring order
slides.body_md: Which officer acts when order breaks down?
slides.narration: Imagine noise in the House. Which officer presides over the Assembly and keeps order?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **Unicameral:** one House; **bicameral:** two Houses; six States have a Council (as of 2024).
A Council is created or abolished by a **law of Parliament** after an Assembly resolution.
Assembly: **directly elected**, **500 at most, 60 at least**, term **five years**.
Member: **citizen, twenty-five, on the roll, no office of profit**; presided by the **Speaker**.

rows: One House or two; six States have a Council (as of 2024)
Not more than 500, not less than 60
Citizen, twenty-five, on the roll, no office of profit

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: unicameral and bicameral, Assembly strength, term, qualifications and the Speaker
visual.caption: Part 1 in one table.

slides.narration: To sum up. A unicameral legislature has one House and a bicameral one has two. Six States have a Council as of two thousand twenty four. A Council is created or abolished by a law of Parliament after the Assembly asks for it. The Assembly is directly elected, serves five years, and is presided over by the Speaker, whom the members elect.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Write **as of 2024** when you name States with a Council.
Give **both** limits of the Assembly: 500 and 60.
Name **who** can dissolve the Assembly and **who** can extend it.
The Speaker is **elected by the members**, not nominated.
Avoid current office-holders; use the **office**, not the person.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Write as of two thousand twenty four when you name the States with a Council. Give both limits on the size of the Assembly. Say who can dissolve the Assembly, and who can extend its term. Remember the Speaker is elected by the members. And speak of the office, not of any person who holds it today.

decks.title: The State Legislature — Part 2: The Legislative Council and the Powers of the Legislature
goals: Explain how members of the Legislative Council are elected or nominated and why it is a permanent House
State the size, term and qualifications of the Council
Describe the legislative, financial, executive-control, electoral and amendment powers of the State legislature
Compare the powers of the Assembly with those of the Council

slides.heading: The Council and the powers of the legislature
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **upper House** and what the legislature **can do**.

nodes.label: The Legislative Council
Term and permanence
Powers of the legislature
Assembly and Council compared

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the composition of the Legislative Council, its term and permanence, the powers of the State legislature, and a comparison of the two Houses
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we study the Legislative Council, the upper House that a few States have. We see how its members are chosen, why it is called a permanent House, and what powers the State legislature has. At the end, we compare the two Houses and see why the Assembly is the stronger one.

slides.heading: The Legislative Council
bullets: Also called the **Vidhan Parishad**, the upper House.
Strength: **not more than one-third** of the Assembly, and **not fewer than forty**.
Presided over by a **Chairman**, elected by its members.

rows: Not more than one-third of the Assembly and not fewer than forty

visual.alt: Table of features of the Legislative Council: another name, strength of not more than one-third of the Assembly and not fewer than forty, a six-year term for each member and a Chairman elected by the members
visual.caption: The Council at a glance.

slides.narration: The Legislative Council, or Vidhan Parishad, is the upper House. Its size depends on the Assembly. It may have at most one third of the number of members of the Assembly, but never fewer than forty. The members elect a Chairman from among themselves, who presides over the Council, just as the Speaker presides over the Assembly.

slides.body_md: Five routes, and the shares add up to a whole.

slides.narration: The Council has a mixed membership. About one third is elected by the members of the Legislative Assembly. About one third is elected by members of local bodies. One twelfth is elected by graduates and one twelfth by teachers. About one sixth is nominated by the Governor. Together, these shares make up the whole Council.

slides.heading: Who sits in the Council?
slides.body_md: The nominated members bring **special knowledge**.

headers: Imagined example of a voter or member
rows: A member of the Assembly votes for Council seats
A councillor of a municipality votes
A graduate living in the State votes
A teacher of a higher school votes
An expert in science or social service is nominated

visual.alt: Table of the five groups that fill a Legislative Council, their shares and an imagined example for each
visual.caption: Five routes into the Council.

slides.narration: Each route has its own voters. A councillor of a municipality votes in the local bodies share, and a graduate or a teacher votes in the share for graduates or teachers. The Governor nominates people with special knowledge or experience, in fields such as literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service.

slides.heading: Quick check: a share of seats
slides.body_md: Work out the seats from a share.
slides.narration: Divide the total number of seats by twelve to find the seats of one twelfth.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: dividing a Council
slides.body_md: Turn each share into a number of seats.
bullets: Step 1 — Take the total number of members.
Step 2 — One-third is the total divided by three.
Step 3 — One-twelfth is divided by twelve; one-sixth by six.
Step 4 — Add the five numbers to check the total.

visual.alt: Table working out an imagined 96-member Council: thirty-two seats each from MLAs and local bodies, eight each from graduates and teachers and sixteen nominated, making ninety-six in all
visual.caption: Worked out for ninety-six seats.

slides.narration: Suppose an imagined Council has ninety six members. One third is thirty two, so the MLAs and the local bodies elect thirty two each. One twelfth is eight, so the graduates and the teachers elect eight each. One sixth is sixteen, and these are the nominated members. Add them up and the total is ninety six, which is a useful check.

slides.heading: Age, term and presiding officer
slides.body_md: The Council asks for **more age** and gives **longer terms**.

rows: Six years for a member; the House is never dissolved

visual.alt: Table comparing the Council and the Assembly on minimum age, term and presiding officer
visual.caption: Age, term and presiding officer.

slides.narration: A member of the Council must be at least thirty years old, five years more than for the Assembly. Each member serves a term of six years. The Council is presided over by a Chairman, while the Assembly has a Speaker. And unlike the Assembly, the Council as a whole is never dissolved, as we shall see on the next slide.

slides.heading: Why is the Council permanent?
slides.body_md: One-third retire **every two years**.

slides.narration: A member serves six years. But the terms are staggered. Every second year, one third of the members retire and one third are newly chosen. So at any time two thirds of the members are experienced, and the Council is never empty. This is why it is called a permanent House. The Governor cannot dissolve the Council as he can the Assembly.

slides.body_md: Does dissolving the Assembly dissolve the Council?

sections.heading: 1. Unicameral and bicameral legislatures
sections.body_md:
- Every State has a **legislature**. In most States it is **unicameral** (the Legislative Assembly alone); in a few it is **bicameral** (the Assembly plus the Legislative Council).
- The Assembly (**Vidhan Sabha**) is the **lower House**; the Council (**Vidhan Parishad**) is the **upper House**.
- **As of 2024** the six bicameral States are Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.
- A Council is **created or abolished** by a **law of Parliament** after the State Assembly passes a **resolution by a special majority**.
- **For** a Council: a second look at bills; room for experienced persons. **Against**: extra cost; possible delay.

key_terms.definition_md: A larger-than-usual majority needed for certain decisions, such as the resolution on a Council.

sections.heading: 2. The Legislative Assembly: composition and term
sections.body_md:
- Members are **directly elected** by the voters from **territorial constituencies**, one from each.
- **Strength:** not more than **500** and not less than **60**; a few small States have fewer by special provision.
- **Reserved seats** for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
- **Term:** five years from the first meeting. An early end is possible: the **Governor** may dissolve it, usually advised by the **Chief Minister**. A longer life is possible only in a **national emergency**, when **Parliament** extends it **one year at a time**.
- The Assembly is the **lower House** and the more powerful House.

sections.heading: 3. Qualifications and the presiding officers of the Assembly
sections.body_md:
- A member must be a **citizen of India**, **at least 25 years old**, **registered on the electoral roll**, and must **not hold an office of profit** under the government. The law lists a few other disqualifications.
- The **Speaker** is **elected by the members** from among themselves, presides over the House, keeps order and decides who speaks. A **Deputy Speaker** is also elected and presides when the Speaker is absent.
- Eligibility questions: check the **age**, the **citizenship**, the **roll** and any **paid government post**; name the condition that fails.

sections.heading: 4. The Legislative Council: composition
sections.body_md:
- **Strength:** not more than **one-third** of the Assembly and **not fewer than 40**.
- **How chosen:** about **one-third** by the **MLAs**; about **one-third** by **local bodies**; **one-twelfth** by **graduates**; **one-twelfth** by **teachers**; about **one-sixth** **nominated by the Governor**.
- The nominated members are persons with special knowledge or practical experience in **literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service**.
- Shares add up: 4/12 + 4/12 + 1/12 + 1/12 + 2/12 = 12/12.
- The **Chairman**, elected by the members, presides.

A member appointed by the Governor, not elected.

- Contrast: the **Assembly** has a **five-year term** and a minimum age of **25**, and can be dissolved.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the Speaker or the members of the Assembly are nominated by the Governor.
- Saying the Council can defeat an ordinary bill for good, or that it can bring down a ministry.
- Forgetting **as of 2024** when naming the six bicameral States.
- Giving only one limit (500) on the size of the Assembly, or mixing the Assembly's minimum age (25) with the Council's (30).
- Mixing up the shares: one-third, one-third, one-twelfth, one-twelfth, one-sixth.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, term or number.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a contrast or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A State whose legislature consists of a Legislative Assembly alone, with no second House, has a legislature that is called

options.text_md: bicameral
unicameral
confederal
tricameral

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** unicameral. One House means unicameral. Bicameral means two Houses. Confederal describes a loose union of states, and tricameral (three Houses) is not the pattern of any Indian State.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, which of these States has a Legislative Council in addition to its Legislative Assembly?

options.text_md: Punjab
Gujarat
Kerala
Karnataka

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Karnataka. Karnataka is among the six States with a Council (the others being Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh). Punjab, Gujarat and Kerala have a single House.

questions.stem_md: How can a State that has only an Assembly come to have a Legislative Council?

options.text_md: Parliament makes a law after the State Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority
The Governor issues an order on the advice of the Chief Minister alone
The Election Commission decides after a general election
The Supreme Court orders it when asked by a citizen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Parliament makes a law after the State Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority. The process starts in the State Assembly, which passes a resolution by a special majority, and ends with a law of Parliament. The Governor, the Election Commission and the courts have no power to create a Council by themselves.

questions.stem_md: A student making a chart of bicameral State legislatures, as of 2024, must leave out one of these States because it has only an Assembly. Which one?

options.text_md: Bihar
Maharashtra
Goa
Uttar Pradesh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Goa. Goa has a unicameral legislature. Bihar, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh each have a Legislative Council, so they belong on the chart.

questions.stem_md: People who favour a second House in a State give several reasons. Which one is a reason in favour of a Legislative Council?

options.text_md: It makes the budget pass faster because two Houses vote on it
It allows the Council to remove the Council of Ministers
It can give a second look to a bill and bring in experienced people who might not win a direct election
It makes the cost of running the legislature lower

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It can give a second look to a bill and bring in experienced people who might not win a direct election. A revising role and the entry of persons with special knowledge are the usual arguments. Two Houses tend to slow, not speed, a bill; the Council of Ministers answers to the Assembly alone; and a second House adds to expense, which is an argument against it.

questions.stem_md: Match each House with its description.

options.text_md: Legislative Assembly
Legislative Council
Unicameral legislature
Bicameral legislature

match_right.text_md: Upper House, a permanent body that is never dissolved
Lower House, members elected directly by voters
A legislature with a single House

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The Assembly is the directly elected lower House, the Council is the permanent upper House, unicameral means one House and bicameral means two.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Even in a unicameral State such as the imagined Tamrapur, a bill that the Assembly has passed does not become a law until the Governor gives assent.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The Governor's assent is the last step in making a State law, whether the legislature has one House or two.

questions.stem_md: Explain the terms unicameral and bicameral as used for State legislatures.
questions.solution_md: One House versus two Houses, with the names of the Houses.

answer.model_answer_md: A **unicameral** legislature has **one House**, the Legislative Assembly, as in most States. A **bicameral** legislature has **two Houses**, the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council, as in the few States that have a Council.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined State of Sindhuvan the Assembly wants a second House. State the steps by which a Legislative Council can be created.
questions.solution_md: Assembly resolution by special majority, then a law of Parliament.

answer.model_answer_md: First the **Sindhuvan Assembly** passes a **resolution** by a **special majority** asking for a Council. Then **Parliament** passes a **law** creating it. A Council can be abolished in the same way.

marking_scheme.step: Assembly resolution by a special majority

questions.stem_md: Give two points in favour of a Legislative Council and one point against it.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons for, one against.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A Council gives a **second look** to hasty bills passed by the Assembly.
2. It brings in **experienced persons**, such as teachers and nominated experts, who may not contest elections.
3. Against: it **adds to the cost** and can **delay** lawmaking, although the Assembly's view finally prevails.

questions.stem_md: How are most members of a State Legislative Assembly chosen?

options.text_md: They are directly elected by voters in territorial constituencies
They are nominated by the Governor
They are elected by members of the Legislative Council
They are chosen by the Chief Minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They are directly elected by voters in territorial constituencies. Voters in each territorial constituency elect one member directly. The Governor does not nominate the members, the Council does not elect them, and the Chief Minister does not choose them.

questions.stem_md: Within which limits does the number of members of a State Legislative Assembly normally lie?

options.text_md: Not more than 250 and not less than 100
Not more than 545 and not less than 100
Not more than 100 and not less than 40
Not more than 500 and not less than 60

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Not more than 500 and not less than 60. An Assembly may have at most 500 and normally at least 60 members. A few small States have fewer by special provision. Figures such as 250 and 545 belong to other Houses, and 40 is the minimum of a Legislative Council.

questions.stem_md: Before its full term ends, a State Legislative Assembly can be dissolved by

options.text_md: the Speaker, on a vote of the Council
the Governor, usually on the advice of the Chief Minister
the Rajya Sabha, by a simple resolution
the Chief Justice of the High Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the Governor, usually on the advice of the Chief Minister. The Governor dissolves the Assembly, acting in practice on the advice of the Chief Minister. The Speaker, the Rajya Sabha and the Chief Justice have no such power.

questions.stem_md: While a national emergency is in operation, the usual five-year term of a State Legislative Assembly can be lengthened by

options.text_md: Parliament, one year at a time
The Governor, by up to five years at once
The Chief Minister, by a cabinet decision
The Speaker, by a ruling

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Parliament, one year at a time. Parliament may extend the term, one year at a time, while a national emergency lasts. The Governor, the Chief Minister and the Speaker have no power to lengthen the term.

questions.stem_md: Meenal Rao of the imagined State of Kolahar is an Indian citizen, is on the voters' list and holds no office of profit, but she is 24 years old. Can she contest for the Legislative Assembly?

options.text_md: Yes, because citizens above 18 can contest any election
No, because a candidate must be at least 25 years old
No, because only members of the Council may contest
Yes, because the age rule applies only to Parliament

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** No, because a candidate must be at least 25 years old. The minimum age to be a member of an Assembly is 25 years, which Meenal has not reached. The age to vote is not the age to contest, and members of the Council do not have the exclusive right to stand.

questions.stem_md: Raghav Iyer of the imagined State of Harsilla is a citizen, 40 years old and on the voters' list, but he is a paid officer of the State government. Why can he not contest for the Legislative Assembly as things stand?

options.text_md: He is older than the maximum age for members
He is not a citizen of the State by birth
He holds an office of profit under the government
He has not been a member of the Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He holds an office of profit under the government. Holding an office of profit disqualifies a person from being a member. There is no maximum age, a person need not be born in the State, and Council membership is not a condition.

questions.stem_md: Members in the imagined Kesarpur Assembly are shouting and the debate has stopped. Which officer will restore order and decide who may speak?

options.text_md: The Governor
The Chief Minister
The Chairman of the Council
The Speaker

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Speaker. The Speaker presides over the Assembly and keeps order. The Governor is not a member of the House, the Chief Minister is the leader of the government, and the Chairman presides over the Council, a different House.

questions.stem_md: A student notices that a few small States have Assemblies with fewer than 60 members. How is this explained?

options.text_md: These States have no elections and the members are nominated
The limit of 60 applies only to Legislative Councils
The Governor of those States may reduce the number each year
A special provision of the Constitution allows a smaller Assembly for a few small States

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A special provision of the Constitution allows a smaller Assembly for a few small States. The Constitution makes special provision for a few small States. Elections are held there too; the figure of 60 is for Assemblies, not Councils; and a Governor cannot change the number at will.

questions.stem_md: A quiz sheet lists four statements about the Legislative Assembly. Which statement is incorrect?

options.text_md: Its normal term is five years
It is presided over by the Speaker
Its members are nominated by the Governor
Its members are elected from territorial constituencies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its members are nominated by the Governor. The members of the Assembly are elected by voters, not nominated by the Governor (the Governor nominates only some members of a Council). The other three statements are correct.

questions.stem_md: The normal term of a State Legislative Assembly is ___ years.
questions.solution_md: The normal term is five years.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A State Legislative Assembly can be dissolved before it has completed five years.

**Reason (R):** No authority can shorten the term of an Assembly once it has been elected.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: the Governor may dissolve the Assembly early, usually on the Chief Minister's advice. R is false for the same reason: an early dissolution is a recognised way of shortening the term.

questions.stem_md: State the normal term of a State Legislative Assembly and say how it can be cut short or extended.
questions.solution_md: Five years, early dissolution, extension in emergency.

answer.model_answer_md: The normal term is **five years**. The **Governor** can **dissolve** it earlier, usually on the Chief Minister's advice. While a **national emergency** lasts, **Parliament** can lengthen the term, **one year at a time**.

marking_scheme.step: Five years and early dissolution by the Governor
Extension by Parliament in an emergency

questions.stem_md: Who presides over a State Legislative Assembly? State how the presiding officer is chosen and one duty of the office.
questions.solution_md: Speaker, election by members, one duty.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Speaker** presides. The Speaker is **elected by the members** of the Assembly from among themselves, with a **Deputy Speaker** to help. One duty is to **maintain order** and conduct the proceedings of the House.

questions.stem_md: Two persons wish to contest the Assembly seat of Nirmal Vale, an imagined constituency: Arvind is 31, a citizen and on its voters' list; Bhavna is 22 and also a citizen on the voters' list. State who is eligible, with a reason.
questions.solution_md: Arvind eligible; Bhavna too young.

answer.model_answer_md: **Arvind** is eligible: he is a **citizen**, over **25 years** and **on the electoral roll**. **Bhavna** is not eligible, because she is **below 25 years**, the minimum age for an Assembly member.

marking_scheme.step: Bhavna not eligible with a reason

questions.stem_md: List three conditions a person must meet to be a member of a State Legislative Assembly, and explain one of them in a line.
questions.solution_md: Three conditions with a short explanation of one.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The person must be a **citizen of India**.
2. The person must be **at least 25 years old**.
3. The person must be **on the electoral roll** and must **not hold an office of profit**; holding a paid government post would create a conflict between duty to the government and duty to the House.

marking_scheme.step: Third condition with a line of explanation

questions.stem_md: What is the minimum age for a member of a State Legislative Council?

options.text_md: 25 years
30 years
35 years
21 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 30 years. A Council member must be at least 30 years old. Twenty-five is the age for the Assembly, 35 is the age for some higher offices, and 21 is not the age rule for either House.

questions.stem_md: In a State Legislative Council, a fixed share of members retires at regular intervals. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: One-third of the members retire every two years
Half of the members retire every year
All members retire together every five years
One-sixth of the members retire every month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** One-third of the members retire every two years. A member serves for six years and one-third of the members retire every second year, so the House continues. Half-yearly or all-at-once retirement describes other bodies, and a monthly retirement has no basis in the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: Which two groups each elect about one-third of the members of a State Legislative Council?

options.text_md: Graduates, and teachers
The members of the Legislative Assembly, and members of local bodies such as municipalities and district boards
The Governor, and the Chief Minister
Members of the Rajya Sabha, and the voters of the State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The members of the Legislative Assembly, and members of local bodies such as municipalities and district boards. About one-third are elected by the MLAs and about one-third by members of local bodies. Graduates and teachers elect one-twelfth each, and the Governor nominates about one-sixth.

questions.stem_md: Lakshmi Devi, an imagined organiser who has built cooperative societies across Dhavalpur for thirty years, has never contested an election. Through which route could she most suitably enter the Legislative Council?

options.text_md: Election by the graduates of the State
Election by the teachers of the State
Direct election in a territorial constituency
Nomination by the Governor of a person with special knowledge of the cooperative movement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Nomination by the Governor of a person with special knowledge of the cooperative movement. About one-sixth of the Council is nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge of fields such as the cooperative movement and social service. The other routes depend on being a graduate, being a teacher, or contesting an election.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined State of Mayurgarh the Council has 96 members. About how many of them are elected by the teachers' constituencies, if the Constitution's share is followed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 8. Teachers elect one-twelfth of the Council, and 96 divided by 12 is 8. The figure 12 would be one-eighth, 16 would be one-sixth (the nominated share), and 32 would be one-third.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Legislative Council described as a permanent House?

options.text_md: Its members are chosen for life
It cannot be abolished by any law
It is never dissolved as a whole, because a part of its members retire every two years
It meets every day of the year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is never dissolved as a whole, because a part of its members retire every two years. The Council is not dissolved; as one-third of the members retire at intervals, the House carries on. Members have a six-year term, not life; a Council can be abolished by Parliament on the Assembly's resolution; and it does not meet every day.

questions.stem_md: The Assembly of the imagined State of Girivan has 240 members. What is the largest number of members its Legislative Council may have?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 80. The Council may have at most one-third of the Assembly, and 240 divided by 3 is 80. The figure 60 is a quarter, 120 is a half, and 240 would make the Council as large as the Assembly.

questions.stem_md: A member of a Legislative Council is chosen for a term of ___ years.
questions.solution_md: The term of a Council member is six years.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the Governor dissolves a State Legislative Assembly, the Legislative Council is dissolved along with it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The Council is a permanent House and is not dissolved, even though the Assembly can be dissolved.

questions.stem_md: Match each item with the number that goes with it.

options.text_md: Minimum age of a Council member
Minimum age of an Assembly member
Term of a Council member
Days a Council may hold a money bill

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Council: age 30 and term 6 years; Assembly: age 25; a money bill may be held for 14 days.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Legislative Council of a State is called a permanent House.

**Reason (R):** One-third of its members retire every two years and are replaced, so the whole House is never dissolved at one time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the staggered retirement of members is exactly why the Council continues without dissolution.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Legislative Council not dissolved like the Assembly? Explain what keeps it going.
questions.solution_md: Permanent House; staggered retirement.

answer.model_answer_md: The Council is a **permanent House**. Members serve **six years**, and **one-third retire every second year**, with new members taking their place. Hence at no time is the whole House **dissolved or empty**.

marking_scheme.step: Council is a permanent House, six-year term

questions.stem_md: State the limits on the size of a Legislative Council. If the Assembly of the imagined State of Dhavalpur has 210 members, what is the greatest possible size of its Council?
questions.solution_md: One-third of the Assembly, minimum 40; 70 for 210.

answer.model_answer_md: A Council may have **at most one-third** of the Assembly's strength and **not fewer than 40** members. For 210 members the largest Council is **210 divided by 3, which is 70**.

questions.stem_md: How are the members of a State Legislative Council elected or nominated? Give the share of each group.
questions.solution_md: Five groups and their shares.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. About **one-third** are elected by the **MLAs** and about **one-third** by members of **local bodies**.
2. **One-twelfth** are elected by **graduates** and **one-twelfth** by **teachers**.
3. About **one-sixth** are **nominated by the Governor** from persons with special knowledge.

questions.stem_md: The Assembly of a bicameral State passes an ordinary bill and sends it to the Council. For how long can the Council delay it the first time?

options.text_md: Up to three months
Up to one year
Up to fourteen days
It can reject the bill for good

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Up to three months. On the first occasion the Council can hold or reject an ordinary bill for up to three months. A year is too long, fourteen days is the limit for a money bill, and the Council has no power to defeat a bill finally.

questions.stem_md: In which House of a bicameral State legislature can a money bill be introduced?

options.text_md: Only in the Legislative Council
In either House
In neither; it is introduced by the Governor
Only in the Legislative Assembly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Only in the Legislative Assembly. Money bills can be introduced only in the Assembly. The Council cannot introduce them, a choice of either House is not allowed, and the Governor does not introduce a bill.

questions.stem_md: A motion of no confidence that can bring down a State government can be passed only in

options.text_md: the Legislative Council
the Legislative Assembly
either House with equal effect
the Governor's office

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the Legislative Assembly. The ministry is responsible to the Assembly, so only the Assembly can defeat it by a no-confidence motion. The Council can question and debate but cannot remove the ministry.

questions.stem_md: To which House is the State Council of Ministers collectively responsible?

options.text_md: The Legislative Assembly
The Legislative Council
Both Houses equally
The Governor alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Legislative Assembly. The Council of Ministers answers to the directly elected Assembly. It is not responsible to the Council, to both Houses equally, or to the Governor alone.

questions.stem_md: Which members of a State legislature take part in electing the President of India?

options.text_md: All members of the Legislative Council
The elected members of the Legislative Assembly
The Speaker alone
The nominated members of the Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The elected members of the Legislative Assembly. The elected members of each State Assembly are part of the electoral college for the President. Members of the Council do not vote in this election, and the Speaker votes as an elected member, not alone.

questions.stem_md: The Assembly of the imagined State of Dhavalpur passes an ordinary bill on regulating weekly markets. The Council rejects it. The Assembly passes the same bill again, and the Council again rejects it or lets a month pass without passing it. What is the position of the bill?

options.text_md: It lapses, because the Council has refused it twice
It goes to the Governor, who must pass it into law as if both Houses had agreed
It is treated as passed by both Houses in the form the Assembly passed it
It must be put before a joint sitting of both Houses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is treated as passed by both Houses in the form the Assembly passed it. On the second passage the Assembly's view prevails: after the Council rejects or delays the bill again, it is deemed passed, and then goes for the Governor's assent. It does not lapse, and a State legislature has no joint sitting to settle such a dispute.

questions.stem_md: The Council of the imagined State of Kesarpur keeps a money bill passed by the Assembly for twenty days without returning it. What is the result?

options.text_md: The bill is dead because the Council did not return it in time
The Assembly must wait until the Council passes it
The Governor sends it to the High Court
The bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Assembly passed it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Assembly passed it. The Council may hold a money bill for only fourteen days. After that, the bill is deemed passed in the form the Assembly passed it. The Council cannot kill it, the Assembly need not wait, and no court is involved.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined State of Sindhuvan a member of the Legislative Council wants to put a question to a minister about village roads. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The member cannot ask any question, because only the Assembly may question ministers
The member can move a no-confidence motion against the minister in the Council
The question can be asked only if the Governor permits it
The member can ask the question in the Council, since both Houses can question ministers, but only the Assembly can remove the ministry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The member can ask the question in the Council, since both Houses can question ministers, but only the Assembly can remove the ministry. Questions and discussion are part of the control that both Houses have over the executive, but the ministry's survival depends on the Assembly alone. The Council can neither move a motion that removes the government nor needs the Governor's permission to put a question.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a bicameral State, the Legislative Council has very little power over a money bill.

**Reason (R):** A money bill can be introduced only in the Legislative Council.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true, since the Council can only hold the bill for fourteen days and make recommendations. R is false, because a money bill can be introduced only in the Assembly.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A no-confidence motion can bring down a State government only if it is passed in the Legislative Assembly.

**Reason (R):** The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

Choose the correct option.

(A) is false and (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Three months, then one month; the Assembly prevails.

questions.stem_md: What is the role of the Legislative Council in the passing of a money bill?
questions.solution_md: Introduced in the Assembly; Council holds it fourteen days.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a no-confidence motion has meaning only in the Legislative Assembly.
questions.solution_md: Responsibility to the Assembly; resignation of the ministry.

marking_scheme.step: Defeat means resignation; Council has no such power

questions.stem_md: Describe the financial powers of the Legislative Assembly, and say how the Council's part in money matters differs.
questions.solution_md: Assembly controls money; Council limited.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **money bill** can be introduced only in the **Assembly**, and the Assembly alone votes on the **demands for grants** in the budget.
2. The **Council** can only **discuss** the budget and **hold a money bill for fourteen days**, making recommendations.
3. The Assembly may **accept or reject** those recommendations, so its view finally prevails.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which the State legislature controls the executive.
questions.solution_md: Questions; motions; no-confidence.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Members put **questions** to ministers and demand answers about their departments.
2. They bring **motions and debates**, such as **adjournment motions**, to draw attention to the government's actions.
3. The **Assembly** can pass a **no-confidence motion** and make the **Council of Ministers resign**.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why the Legislative Assembly is a more powerful House than the Legislative Council.
questions.solution_md: Money bills, ordinary bills, responsibility of the ministry.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The Assembly alone can **introduce money bills**; the Council can only hold them for 14 days.
2. On ordinary bills the Council can only **delay**, and the **Assembly's view prevails**.
3. The **Council of Ministers is responsible to the Assembly**, so only the Assembly can remove a ministry.

questions.stem_md: The Assembly of the imagined State of Kolahar passes a bill raising taxes on weekly markets. The Council, which has a majority from the opposite side, wishes to stop it. What can it do and what can it not do? Give your reasoning.
questions.solution_md: Money versus ordinary bill; delay only.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. If the bill is a **money bill**, the Council can only **hold it for fourteen days** and make recommendations.
2. If it is an **ordinary bill**, the Council can **delay it** for three months and then one month more.
3. It **cannot stop the bill for good**, as the **Assembly's view finally prevails**.

questions.stem_md:
Some State legislatures have two Houses and others have one.

(i) Explain the terms unicameral and bicameral, naming the Houses of a bicameral State. **[3]**
(ii) Name any three States that have a Legislative Council (as of 2024) and say how a State can get or lose a Council. **[3]**
(iii) Give two arguments for and two against having a Legislative Council. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and Houses; States and procedure; arguments for and against.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **unicameral** legislature has one House, the **Legislative Assembly**. A **bicameral** legislature has two Houses, the **Legislative Assembly** (lower House) and the **Legislative Council** (upper House).

(ii) As of 2024, **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Karnataka** (also Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh) have a Council. The **State Assembly** passes a **resolution by a special majority**, and **Parliament** then makes a **law** to create or abolish the Council.

(iii) For: it gives a **second look** at hasty bills; it brings in **experienced people**. Against: it is an **extra cost**; it can **delay** lawmaking, and it is not directly elected.

questions.stem_md:
The Legislative Assembly is the more important House of a State legislature.

(i) Explain its composition and how its members are elected. **[3]**
(ii) State its term, and explain how the term may be shortened or lengthened. **[3]**
(iii) State four qualifications for membership of the Legislative Assembly. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition and election; term and its change; four qualifications.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Assembly has **not more than 500 and not less than 60 members** (a few small States have fewer). They are **directly elected** by the voters from **territorial constituencies**, with seats **reserved** for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It is presided over by the **Speaker**.

(ii) The normal term is **five years**. The **Governor** may **dissolve** it earlier, usually on the **Chief Minister's advice**. While a **national emergency** lasts, **Parliament** can lengthen the term, **one year at a time**.

(iii) A member must be a **citizen of India**, at least **25 years old**, **registered as a voter** on the electoral roll, and must **not hold an office of profit** under the government.

questions.stem_md:
A few States have a Legislative Council, the upper House of the State legislature.

(i) Explain how its members are elected or nominated, naming any three groups with their shares. **[3]**
(ii) State the minimum age of a member, the term of office and the limits on the size of the Council. **[3]**
(iii) Why is the Legislative Council called a permanent House? How does this differ from the Assembly? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition; age, term and size; permanent House.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **One-third** are elected by the **MLAs**, **one-third** by members of **local bodies**, **one-twelfth** by **graduates**, **one-twelfth** by **teachers**, and about **one-sixth** are **nominated by the Governor** from persons with special knowledge.

(ii) A member must be at least **30 years old**. The term is **six years**. The Council can have **not more than one-third** of the Assembly's strength and **not fewer than 40** members.

(iii) The Council is **never dissolved as a whole**. **One-third** of the members **retire every two years** and new members take their place, so there is always a House. The **Assembly**, in contrast, serves a **five-year term** and may be **dissolved** by the Governor.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Permanent because of retirement by thirds

questions.stem_md:
The State legislature has a wide range of powers.

(i) Explain its legislative powers. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the financial powers of the State legislature, with special reference to a money bill. **[3]**
(iii) Explain its control over the executive and its electoral functions. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Legislative; financial; executive control and electoral.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The legislature makes laws on the subjects of the **State List** and the **Concurrent List**. A bill is passed by the Assembly (and by the Council, where there is one) and becomes law with the **Governor's assent**. The Council can only **delay** an ordinary bill.

(ii) A **money bill** can start only in the **Assembly**; the Assembly alone votes on the **demands for grants**. The Council can only **keep a money bill for fourteen days**, with recommendations.

(iii) Members ask **questions**, move **motions** and the **Assembly** can pass a **no-confidence motion**, as the ministry is **responsible to it**. The elected **MLAs** take part in electing the **President** and elect the State's **Rajya Sabha** members. State legislatures also **ratify certain amendments**.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Passage of a bill and Governor's assent
(ii) Money bill and grants in the Assembly

questions.stem_md:
A bicameral State legislature has an Assembly and a Council.

(i) Distinguish the two Houses in the way their members come to the House. **[3]**
(ii) Distinguish them in term of office and minimum age. **[3]**
(iii) Explain, with two reasons, why the Assembly is more powerful than the Council. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition; term and age; reasons for the Assembly's greater power.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Assembly** members are **directly elected** by voters from constituencies. **Council** members are **indirectly elected** by MLAs, local bodies, graduates and teachers, and about one-sixth are **nominated by the Governor**.

(ii) The Assembly has a **five-year term** and a minimum age of **25**; it can be **dissolved**. The Council has a **six-year term** for each member, a minimum age of **30**, and is a **permanent House**.

(iii) First, the **money bill** begins only in the Assembly and the Council can only hold it for **fourteen days**. Second, the ministry is **responsible to the Assembly**, which alone can pass a **no-confidence motion**. Besides, on ordinary bills the Council can only delay and the Assembly finally prevails.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined State of Vaidhara has a bicameral legislature and its Assembly has 150 members. The Assembly passes (1) a money bill on a levy for local fairs and (2) an ordinary bill on the registration of weekly markets, which the Council rejects. A group of members from the Assembly also wishes to remove the ministry.

(i) What is the greatest number of members the Vaidhara Council may have? Show your working. **[3]**
(ii) What can the Council do with each of the two bills, and what is the final result? **[3]**
(iii) In which House can the removal of the ministry be attempted, and why not in the other? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Maximum Council size; fate of each bill; where the ministry can be removed.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Council may have **at most one-third** of the Assembly's members. One-third of **150** is **50**, which is above the minimum of **40**, so the greatest number is **50**.

(ii) The **money bill** can be **held for only fourteen days**, after which it is treated as passed in the form the Assembly passed it. The **ordinary bill** can be **delayed three months** on the first occasion; if the Assembly passes it again and the Council again opposes it for a month, the bill is **treated as passed**. The **Assembly prevails** in both cases.

(iii) The attempt can be made only in the **Assembly**, through a **no-confidence motion**, because the **Council of Ministers is responsible to the Assembly**. The Council can **question** and **debate**, but has **no power to remove** the government.

questions.stem_md:
The Assembly of the imagined State of Mayurgarh is debating whether to ask for its Legislative Council to be abolished.

(i) Explain the steps by which a Council can be abolished. **[3]**
(ii) Give one argument for keeping the Council and one argument for abolishing it. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate which House's view prevails in a disagreement, and state whether you think the Council should be kept, giving a reason. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Procedure; arguments; evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **State Assembly** passes a **resolution** by a **special majority**, asking for abolition. Then **Parliament** passes a **law** abolishing the Council. The process is the same as the creation of a Council.

(ii) **For keeping:** the Council gives a **second look** to bills and brings in **experienced members**. **For abolishing:** it **adds to the cost**, may **delay** useful laws, and **does not answer directly** to the voters.

(iii) The **Assembly's view prevails**: the Council can delay an ordinary bill for only a limited time and has little say over a money bill. A balanced view is that a Council is useful for **careful revision**, but because its power is limited its value depends on the **quality of its members**; whichever view is taken, a reasoned answer is needed.

questions.stem_md: The Governor of the imagined State of Mayurgarh dissolved the Assembly two years after it was elected, and fresh elections were held. What is the normal term of the newly elected Assembly?

options.text_md: The remaining three years of the old term
A fresh term of five years
Six years, like the Council
Two years, to make up the time lost

questions.stem_md: In the imagined bicameral State of Girivan the Governor has just dissolved the Assembly. What is the position of the Legislative Council?

options.text_md: It continues, because it is a permanent House that is never dissolved
It is dissolved along with the Assembly
It becomes the only House, and all its members retire at once
It is suspended until the Chief Minister is re-elected

questions.stem_md: A member of the Legislative Council of the imagined State of Dhavalpur tries to introduce the State's Finance Bill in the Council. What is the position?
